{{short description|Abelian group, in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], especially [[differential topology]] and [[cobordism theory]], a '''Kervaire–Milnor group''' is an [[abelian group]] defined as the [[h-cobordism]] classes of [[Homotopy sphere|homotopy spheres]] with the [[connected sum]] as composition and the reverse [[Orientability|orientation]] as inversion. It controls the existence of smooth structures on [[Topological manifold|topological]] and [[Piecewise linear manifold|piecewise linear]] (PL) manifolds.<ref>Lück 2004, p. 119</ref> Concerning the related question of PL structures on topological manifolds, the obstruction is given by the [[Kirby–Siebenmann invariant]], which is a lot easier to understand. In all but three and four dimensions, Kervaire–Milnor groups furthermore give the possible smooth structures on spheres, hence [[Exotic sphere|exotic spheres]]. They are named after the French mathematician [[Michel Kervaire]] and the American mathematician [[John Milnor]], who first described them in 1962. (Their paper was originally only supposed to be the first part, but a second part was never published.)

== Definition ==
An important property of [[Sphere|spheres]] is their neutrality with respect to the [[connected sum]] of manifolds.<ref name=":1">Kevaire & Milnor 1962, Lemma 4.5</ref> Expanding this [[monoid]] structure with a [[Operation (mathematics)|composition]] and a [[neutral element]] to a group structure requires the restriction on manifolds, for which a connected sum can result in a sphere, hence which intuitively doesn't have holes. This is possible with [[Homotopy sphere|homotopy spheres]], which are closed smooth manifolds with the same homotopy type as a sphere, with restriction to h-cobordism classes being useful for application. Inversion is then given by changing their orientation,<ref name=":1" /> which results in a group structure.<ref>Kevaire & Milnor 1962, Theorem 1.1</ref>

An alternative definition in higher dimensions is given by the description of topological, PL and smooth structures. Let <math>\operatorname{Top}_n</math> be the [[topological group]] of [[Homeomorphism|homeomorphisms]], <math>\operatorname{PL}_n</math> the topological group of PL homeomorphisms and <math>\operatorname{Diff}_n</math> be the topological group of [[Diffeomorphism|diffeomorphisms]] of [[euclidean space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>. An [[inductive limit]] yields topological groups <math>\operatorname{Top}</math>, <math>\operatorname{PL}</math> and <math>\operatorname{Diff}</math> (which is [[homotopy equivalent]] to the infinite [[orthogonal group]] <math>\operatorname{O}(\infty)</math>), for which [[Classifying space|classifying spaces]] can be regarded. For a topological manifold <math>X</math>, its tangent bundle <math>TX</math> is also a topological manifold, which is classified by a continuous map <math>X\rightarrow\operatorname{BTop}</math>. Analogous for a PL and a smooth manifold, there are classifying maps <math>X\rightarrow\operatorname{BPL}</math> and <math>X\rightarrow\operatorname{BDiff}</math> respectively. The canonical inclusions <math>\operatorname{BDiff}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{BPL}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{BTop}</math> show that every smooth is a PL and every PL is a topological structure.

The Kervaire–Milnor groups are then alternatively given by the [[Homotopy group|homotopy groups]] of the [[Quotient group|quotient groups]]  <math>\operatorname{PL}/\operatorname{Diff}</math> and <math>\operatorname{Top}/\operatorname{Diff}</math>:<ref name=":6">Freed & Uhlenbeck 1991, p. 12–13</ref>

: <math>
\Theta_n
\cong\pi_n\left(\operatorname{PL}/\operatorname{Diff}\right)
\cong\pi_n\left(\operatorname{Top}/\operatorname{Diff}\right)
</math>

for <math>
n\geq 5
</math>.

== Examples ==
Some low-dimensional Kervaire–Milnor groups are given by:<ref>Kevaire & Milnor 1962, p. 504</ref><ref>Freed & Uhlenbeck 1991, p. 12–13</ref>

: <math>
\Theta_1\cong 1
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_2\cong 1
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_3\cong 1
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_4\cong 1
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_5\cong 1
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_6\cong 1
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_7\cong\mathbb{Z}_{28}
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_8\cong\mathbb{Z}_2
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_9\cong\mathbb{Z}_2^2
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_{10}\cong\mathbb{Z}_6
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_{11}\cong\mathbb{Z}_{992}
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_{14}\cong\mathbb{Z}_2
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_{16}\cong\mathbb{Z}_2
</math>
: <math>
\Theta_{61}\cong 1
</math>

After the construction of Milnor spheres in 1956, it was already known that Kervaire–Milnor groups don't have to be trivial with the more exact result <math>
\Theta_7\cong\mathbb{Z}_{28}
</math> only having been concluded the following years. A generating exotic sphere was constructed by [[Egbert Brieskorn]] as special case of a [[Brieskorn manifold]] in 1966. It possesses more unique properties and is also called [[Gromoll–Meyer sphere]].

It is still unknown (in 2025) whether exotic spheres exist in four dimensions with the result <math>
\Theta_4\cong 1
</math> not allowing any conclusion about it. This is because Kervaire–Milnor groups also only describe the diffeomorphism classes of spheres for <math>
n\neq 3,4
</math>. Often, the set of diffeomorphism classes of homotopy spheres is denoted <math>
\overline\Theta_n
</math> with the canonical forgetful map <math>
\overline\Theta_n\rightarrow\Theta_n
</math> then being bijective for <math>
n\neq 3,4
</math>.<ref>Lück 2004, Lemma 6.2</ref>

== Properties ==

* All Kervaire–Milnor groups are finite. Michel Kervaire and John Milnor already proved this in their original paper for <math>
n\neq 3
</math> with the remaining case <math>
n=3
</math> being solved by the proof of the [[Poincaré conjecture]] by [[Grigori Perelman]].
* <math>
\Theta_1
</math>, <math>
\Theta_3
</math>, <math>
\Theta_5
</math> and <math>
\Theta_{61}
</math> are the only trivial Kervaire–Milnor groups in odd dimensions.<ref>Wang & Xu 2017</ref>
